lead: A plucked guitar string, a bridge cable and a sitar string all carry a disturbance that travels along them. This chapter writes the equation that any such disturbance must obey, the wave equation, and solves it for a stretched string. From the equation comes the speed v = √(T/μ), where T is tension and μ is mass per metre. The same equation, with a different speed, governs light in Unit 3, so the pattern learned here is reused everywhere.
prereq: You need: 2.1 Simple harmonic motion for ω and phase, and Newton's second law from Unit 1, Mechanics and Properties of Matter.

sections.h3: The wave equation from a small element

blocks.text: Stretch a string along the x-axis and hold it under tension. The tension T (newton, N) is the force each part of the string exerts on the part beside it, always along the string. The string has linear density μ (kilogram per metre, kg/m). Pluck it sideways and the string moves up and down: y(x, t) is the sideways displacement in metres of the point at position x metres at time t seconds. The motion is transverse, across the string's own length.

Take a short piece of the string between x and x + Δx. Tension pulls on it at both ends, along the tangents. Assume the slope ∂y/∂x is small, so the tension has the same magnitude T everywhere and the tangent angle θ obeys sin θ ≈ tan θ = ∂y/∂x.

Upward force at the right end = T(∂y/∂x) at x + Δx. Upward force at the left end = −T(∂y/∂x) at x. Net upward force = T[(∂y/∂x) at x + Δx − (∂y/∂x) at x] = T (∂²y/∂x²) Δx, using the definition of the derivative.
The mass of the piece is μ Δx and its upward acceleration is ∂²y/∂t². Newton's second law gives T (∂²y/∂x²) Δx = μ Δx (∂²y/∂t²). Cancel Δx:

blocks.where: y is transverse displacement (m); x is position along the string (m); t is time (s); μ is linear density (kg/m); T is tension (N).

blocks.text: Every wave equation has the form ∂²y/∂x² = (1/v²) ∂²y/∂t², with v the wave speed. Comparing the two, 1/v² = μ/T, so v = √(T/μ). Nothing was assumed about the shape of the wave: the equation fell out of the forces alone.

sections.h3: Travelling waves and the sine wave

blocks.text: The wave equation is solved by any function whose argument is x − vt or x + vt:
y(x, t) = f(x − vt) + g(x + vt)
blocks.where: f is a shape travelling in the +x direction; g is a shape travelling in the −x direction; v is the speed (m/s).

blocks.text: Why: if you walk along at speed v in +x, the quantity x − vt stays fixed, so f is a rigid shape sliding along at speed v without changing form. The g term is the same picture going the other way. The string never moves forward; only the shape moves.
The most useful choice is sinusoidal:

blocks.where: A is the amplitude (m); k = 2π/λ is the wave number (rad/m); λ is the wavelength (m); ω = 2πf is the angular frequency (rad/s); f is the frequency (Hz); φ is the starting phase (rad).

blocks.text: Hold the phase kx − ωt fixed. As t grows, x must grow to keep it fixed, and dx/dt = ω/k. So v = ω/k = fλ. One full wavelength passes a given point every period T₀ = 1/f seconds. Here T₀ is the period in seconds, not the tension T in newton.

Example: y = sin(x − t) with x in metres has k = 1 rad/m, ω = 1 rad/s and speed 1 m/s. At t = 0 a crest sits at x = 1.57 m; at t = 1 s the same crest sits at x = 2.57 m. The shape has shifted by 1 m, which is v × t.
Some books write A sin(ωt − kx) or A sin(2π(t/T − x/λ)). The sign choice only fixes where the phase starts; the speed and shape are the same.

sections.h3: Speed, tension and reflection at the ends

blocks.text: The result v = √(T/μ) says three things.

items: Tighter string, faster wave: doubling T multiplies v by √2 = 1.41.
Heavier string, slower wave: μ is mass per metre, not the total mass.
Speed does not depend on amplitude or on how hard you pluck, as long as the slope stays small.

blocks.text: On a guitar or a sitar, the tuning peg changes T and the finger changes the vibrating length; both change the note, through v and through the fixed-end condition described in 2.5.

At a fixed end the string cannot move, so a reflected crest returns as a trough; this is a phase change of π rad. At a free end, such as a ring sliding on a smooth rod, the end can move and the pulse returns upright, with no phase change. That is why a pulse sent down a rope tied to a wall comes back on the other side of the rope's axis.

The same wave equation and the same speed formula v = √(B/ρ) apply to sound in a pipe, where B is the bulk modulus (Pa) and ρ is the density (kg/m³). Pressure and displacement swap nodes and antinodes, so their reflection behaviour at a closed end is opposite (see 2.6). Unit 3 writes the identical equation for electric and magnetic fields, with v replaced by c.

figure.caption: At t = 0 the wave is sin x; one second later the same shape has slid 1 m to the right, so the speed is ω/k = 1 m/s.

spec.aria: The same sine shape shifted to the right at a later time, showing a wave travelling along the string.

examples.question: A string 1.5 m long has mass 0.030 kg and is stretched to a tension of 120 N. It is fixed at both ends. Find (i) the linear density, (ii) the wave speed, (iii) the wavelength of the fundamental mode, (iv) the fundamental frequency.
steps: Linear density is total mass divided by length: μ = m/L = 0.030 kg / 1.5 m = 0.020 kg/m.
Speed from tension and linear density: v = √(T/μ) = √(120 / 0.020) = √6000 = 77.46 m/s.
In the fundamental mode one half-wavelength fits between the two fixed ends (see 2.5), so λ = 2L = 2 × 1.5 m = 3.0 m.
Then v = fλ gives f = v/λ = 77.46 m/s ÷ 3.0 m = 25.82 Hz.
examples.check:
m = 0.030
L = 1.5
T = 120.0
mu = m / L
v = (T / mu) ** 0.5
lam = 2 * L
f = v / lam
print(round(mu, 3))
print(round(v, 2))
print(round(lam, 2))
print(round(f, 2))

traps: Using the total mass m in place of μ = m/L. Putting 0.030 into v = √(T/μ) gives √(120/0.030) = 63.25 m/s, too small by a factor √L = √1.5 = 1.22; μ must be mass per metre, not total mass.
Mixing units: T must be in newton and μ in kg/m. A mass quoted in grams must be divided by 1000 first.
Treating v = √(T/μ) and v = fλ as rival formulas. The first fixes the speed from the medium; the second only links v, f and λ, so you still need the length to get f.
Thinking the string itself moves along its length. Only the pattern moves; each bit of string moves transversely.
Dropping the 2π: k = 2π/λ and ω = 2πf, so v = ω/k, never ω × k.

quiz.q: State the wave equation for a stretched string and define each symbol.
quiz.a: ∂²y/∂x² = (1/v²) ∂²y/∂t², where y is transverse displacement (m), x is position (m), t is time (s) and v is the wave speed (m/s). For a string under tension T and linear density μ, v = √(T/μ).

quiz.q: Write the expression for wave speed on a string and give the SI unit of each quantity.
quiz.a: v = √(T/μ); T in newton (N), μ in kg/m, v in m/s.

quiz.q: Two strings have the same tension but one has twice the linear density. Why is its wave slower?
quiz.a: The restoring force per unit length is the same, but there is twice the mass to accelerate, so the acceleration for a given curvature is halved. v = √(T/μ) then falls by a factor √2 = 1.41.

quiz.q: A pulse travels down a string and reflects from a fixed end. What returns, and why?
quiz.a: An inverted pulse returns. The fixed point cannot move, so the incident and reflected displacements must cancel there at all times; that needs a phase change of π rad, which turns a crest into a trough.

quiz.q: A string has μ = 0.010 kg/m and tension 90 N. Find the wave speed and the frequency of a wave of wavelength 0.60 m on it.
A wave on a string is y = 0.02 sin(6x − 400t), with x in metres and t in seconds. Find A, k, ω, λ, f and v.
quiz.a: A = 0.02 m, k = 6 rad/m, ω = 400 rad/s. λ = 2π/k = 1.047 m, f = ω/2π = 63.66 Hz, v = ω/k = 66.67 m/s (also fλ).

quiz.q: Two strings of equal length are held at the same tension, but one has double the linear density. Compare their wave speeds and their fundamental frequencies.
quiz.a: v ∝ 1/√μ, so the heavier string carries waves at 1/√2 = 0.707 times the speed. With both fixed at the ends the fundamental wavelength is 2L for each, so f = v/2L also falls by 0.707.

quiz.q: Show that y = f(x − vt) satisfies the wave equation.
quiz.a: Let u = x − vt. Then ∂y/∂x = f′(u) and ∂²y/∂x² = f″(u). Also ∂y/∂t = −v f′(u) and ∂²y/∂t² = v² f″(u). Substituting: f″ = (1/v²)(v² f″) = f″, so the equation holds for any twice-differentiable f.

beyond: Not for the exam. The string equation is the one-dimensional member of a family used for overhead power lines swaying in wind, for cables on suspension bridges, and for the basilar membrane inside the ear. Adding bending stiffness turns it into the Euler–Bernoulli beam equation, which civil engineers use for bridge decks and railway tracks. Seismologists solve a two- and three-dimensional version to map rock layers from shot records. The Schrödinger equation of Unit 6 is not this equation, but it shares the same second derivative in x, which is why its solutions are also called waves. Search next: 'd'Alembert solution of the wave equation', 'Euler–Bernoulli beam', 'transverse waves on a cable'.
